title: Begin at the bottom maxim; the well story
description: Clara Grove recounts a father's advice to begin any task at the bottom, told through the story of a man marking out and digging a new well with his two sons. The transcript of this opening is fragmentary.

title: Women's clothing of earlier years; shoes, corsets and dresses
description: Clara Grove describes clothing of past decades, beginning with the cost and durability of shoes and going layer by layer through women's underwear, corsets with whalebone and lacing, corset covers, petticoats, and long skirts. She notes that most garments were homemade.

title: Men's clothing; collars, long underwear, and suits
description: She turns to men's attire, describing standing collars, pull-over shirts, long factory-made underwear worn year round, and three-piece padded suits in plain colors. She recalls her brother scandalizing her by going to work without a hat around 1902.

title: Clothing and morals; the process of aging
description: Clara Grove argues that clothing influences people's mental and moral level. She then answers a question about aging, describing her recent illness, her stubbornness about giving up activities, a doctor's warning that to quit is to be through, and the friends who nursed her.

title: Keeping thoughts forward; Goodwill work; childhood visiting
description: She describes disciplining herself not to dwell on the past and explains her five-day-a-week volunteer work for Goodwill Industries, whose territory runs from Walla Walla to Missoula. She contrasts this with childhood evenings of family visiting and homemade games.

title: Farming yields; rainmakers and county schemes
description: She mentions twelve-bushel wheat yields and dust mulch, squaw corn grown for farm dinners, and the rainmakers of her childhood. She tells of one man's attempt to patent a cover for a whole county, observing that such confidence men have always existed.

title: The town college and its fire; Girl Fisher; memory in old age
description: Clara Grove describes the town's thirty-story college building and recalls the night it burned, when a classmate nicknamed Girl Fisher calmly carried out his crochet work as the building fell. She then muses on her own forgetfulness, keeping memories, and putting past tragedies aside.

title: Women's liberation; trousers and femininity; judging what is inside
description: The group discusses women's liberation, which Clara Grove thinks a good thing carried too far. She tells of wearing knickers on a walking tour and dislikes women abandoning dresses, while agreeing that what matters is what is inside a person.

title: Every person's place in the sun; skilled workers
description: She reflects that all people are equal at the root and that everyone seeks a place in the sun, which others should help them find. She gives examples of a carpenter who fitted moldings without measuring and a dressmaking teacher trained in New York, and closes saying no honest work is beneath anyone.

title: Closing arrangements; the end-of-the-world sect
description: Clara Grove and the interviewer arrange the next session with reminder postcards. By way of stopping, she retells a story from seventy-five years earlier of a sect that gave away its possessions, waited in vain on a hillside for the end of the world, and returned home to its neighbors' scorn.

title: Blizzard of 1888; runaway team at the artesian well
description: Clara Grove recalls living through the hard winters and blizzard of 1888 in South Dakota. She tells how her brother drove a team hauling water from the town's new artesian well, and the horses bolted, forcing him to pull himself into the wagon and ride it home.

title: Neighbor sheltered; schoolteacher frozen
description: A neighbor, Mr. Merlin, stumbled into their kitchen disoriented, and her father kept him at the stove until the three-day blizzard passed. Grove also tells of a schoolteacher found frozen to death in her schoolhouse beside an unfired stove.

title: North Dakota blizzard; saving the stock
description: During a blizzard in North Dakota, Grove and her little brother got the cattle and chickens into the barn just before the storm struck, and the dog arrived at the door caked with snow. On the second day she crawled along a wind-swept ridge to the barn to offer her pony water, which the animals refused, while the storm lasted three days.

title: Montana snowstorms; walking home after dark
description: Grove recounts heavy snowstorms in Montana years later, including one on Memorial Day that dropped nearly two feet of snow. She then describes being brought home late by a neighbor and walking the rest of the way through pastures and barbed wire after dark.
